elements.id-string-8: Rigorous and interactive class discussions that support students to engage in high-level thinking and reasoning are essential to learningand are a central component of most teaching interventions.
elements.id-string-9: However, formally assessing discussion quality ‘at scale’ is expensive and infeasible for most researchers.
elements.id-string-10: In this work, we experimented with various modern natural language processing (NLP)  techniques to automatically generate rubric scores for individual dimensions of classroom text discussion quality.
elements.id-string-11: Specifically, we worked on a  dataset of 90 classroom discussion transcripts consisting of over 18000 turns annotated with fine-grained Analyzing Teaching Moves (ATM) codes and focused on four Instructional Quality Assessment (IQA) rubrics.Despite the limited amount of data, our work shows encouraging results in some of the rubrics while suggesting that there is room for improvement in the others.
elements.id-string-12: We also found that certain NLP approaches work better for certain rubrics.\keywords{Classroom discussion  \and Quality assessment \and NLP}

elements.id-string-67: Specifically, for each sentence, these  models will predict 1 of 6 \textit{ATM} code labels in column 4 of Table \ref{tab:data}.
elements.id-string-70: We hypothesize that it would be easier to separate \textit{Others} from the 5 focal \textit{ATM} codes as they have specific usages.
elements.id-string-71: We perform a 2-step hierarchical classification at sentence level as follows.
elements.id-string-72: Step 1, binary classification, is to classify \textit{Other} versus \textit{5 focal ATM Codes}.
elements.id-string-73: If the code is not \textit{Others}, step 2 is to perform another 5-way classification to identify the final label.
elements.id-string-74: We train separate BERT-based classifiers for each step.
elements.id-string-75: The input for the classifiers is the current sentence concatenated with previous sentences in the same turn and sentences from one previous turn.
elements.id-string-76: Because each \textit{ATM} code except \textit{Others} can be only from one speaker, either Teacher or Student, we train two classifiers for the 5-way classification  of Step 2, one classifier used to predict teacher codes (\textit{Recap or Synthesize S Ideas} and \textit{Press}) and one classifier specialized in student codes (\textit{Strong Link}, \textit{Strong Text-Based Evidence} and \textit{Strong Explanation}).
elements.id-string-77: Depending on  the speaker, only one of them is called for Step 2.
elements.id-string-79: A classroom discussion can be considered as a sequence of sentences.
elements.id-string-80: This approach assigns a label (1 out of the 6 \textit{ATM} codes) to each sentence in a conversation.
elements.id-string-81: Unlike the Hierarchical Classification approach that predicts the label of each sentence independently, in this approach, the label of a given sentence is more dependent on the labels of nearby sentences.
elements.id-string-82: We use BERT-BiLSTM-CRF as our sequence labeling model.
elements.id-string-83: BiLSTM-CRF has been widely used for sequence labeling tasks \cite{lstm_crf_2}
elements.id-string-84: and BERT \cite{bert} provides a powerful tool for sentence representation that can work well with that architecture.
elements.id-string-86: During \textit{ATM} classification, since \textit{Others} constitutes more than 90\% of the total labels, we {\bf downsample} the training data to reduce the imbalance.
elements.id-string-87: For \textit{IQA}  classification, annotators tend to group consecutive sentences sharing the same functionality in one turn as one \textit{ATM} code (e.g., one \textit{Strong Texted-Based Evidence} code is used for two sentences in the excerpt in Section \ref{sec:background}), but our prediction is done on sentence level.
elements.id-string-88: {\bf Merging adjacent \textit{ATM} predictions that are the same into one code} in the inference phase helps preserve this nature.
elements.id-string-89: Also, since the range of the \textit{IQA}  scores is very small (1 to 4), translating the absolute counting of \textit{ATM} codes to \textit{IQA} scores (see Section \ref{sec:background}) can drastically shift the \textit{IQA} scores due to misclassification of the \textit{ATM} codes.
elements.id-string-90: To alleviate this sensitivity, we  build separate {\bf linear regression models to estimate each \textit{IQA}  score from the counting of relevant \textit{ATM} codes}, then use the nearest integers as the \textit{IQA}  scores.
